exam.title: Numerical Mathematics - Advanced Exam
exam.subtitle: Algorithms, approximation and error analysis
exam.instructions: Complete all tasks thoroughly. Provide algorithms explicitly and perform error analyses. Permitted aids: non-programmable calculator.

exercises.title: Newton's method
exercises.description: Determine $\sqrt3$ as a root of $f(x) = x^2 - 3$ with Newton's method and starting value $x_0 = 2$ (two steps). Give the iteration rule and the error.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Iteration rule
$x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)} = x_n - \frac{x_n^2 - 3}{2x_n} = \frac12\left(x_n + \frac{3}{x_n}\right)$.

Step 3: Error
$\sqrt3 = 1.7320508$. Error: $x_0$: $0.268$; $x_1$: $0.0179$; $x_2$: $9.2\cdot10^{-5}$. The number of correct digits roughly doubles per step: **quadratic convergence**.

Step 4: Check and prerequisites
$1.732143^2 = 3.000319$, so $|f(x_2)| \approx 3\cdot10^{-4}$ ✓. Newton needs a good starting value and $f'(x_n) \neq 0$; for $f(x) = x^2 - a$ it is Heron's method.

exercises.title: Lagrange interpolation
exercises.description: Determine the interpolation polynomial through $(0,1), (1,3), (2,2)$ in Lagrange form and monomial form and evaluate it at $x = 0.5$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Lagrange basis polynomials
$L_0 = \frac{(x-1)(x-2)}{(0-1)(0-2)} = \frac{(x-1)(x-2)}{2}$, $L_1 = \frac{x(x-2)}{(1)(-1)} = -x(x-2)$, $L_2 = \frac{x(x-1)}{2}$. Property: $L_i(x_j) = \delta_{ij}$.

Step 2: Lagrange form
$p(x) = 1\cdot L_0 + 3\cdot L_1 + 2\cdot L_2 = \frac{(x-1)(x-2)}{2} - 3x(x-2) + x(x-1)$.

Step 3: Monomial form
Expanding: $\frac12x^2 - \frac32x + 1 - 3x^2 + 6x + x^2 - x = -\frac32x^2 + \frac72x + 1$.

Step 4: Check and evaluation
$p(0) = 1$ ✓, $p(1) = -1.5 + 3.5 + 1 = 3$ ✓, $p(2) = -6 + 7 + 1 = 2$ ✓. $p(0.5) = -0.375 + 1.75 + 1 = 2.375$. Remember: through $n + 1$ points with distinct $x$-values there is exactly one polynomial of degree $\leq n$.

exercises.title: Trapezoidal and Simpson rule
exercises.description: Approximate $\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+x^2}$ with the trapezoidal rule and Simpson's rule, each with $2$ subintervals, and compare with the exact value $\frac\pi4$.
solutionSteps:
Step 2: Trapezoidal rule
$T = \frac h2\big(f_0 + 2f_1 + f_2\big) = 0.25\cdot(1 + 1.6 + 0.5) = 0.775$.

Step 3: Simpson's rule
$S = \frac h3\big(f_0 + 4f_1 + f_2\big) = \frac{0.5}{3}(1 + 3.2 + 0.5) = 0.78333$.

Step 4: Error comparison
Exact: $\frac\pi4 \approx 0.785398$. Trapezoidal error: $0.0104$, Simpson error: $0.0021$. Simpson is considerably more accurate (error $\sim h^4$ versus $\sim h^2$; exact for polynomials up to degree $3$).

Step 5: Check on a known integral
$\int_0^2x^2\,dx = \frac83 \approx 2.667$: Simpson with $h = 1$: $\frac13(0 + 4 + 4) = \frac83$ exact ✓; trapezoidal: $\frac12(0 + 2 + 4) = 3$ (error $0.33$).

exercises.title: LU decomposition with pivoting
exercises.description: Solve $A\vec x = \vec b$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$, $\vec b = (5,6)^T$ using LU decomposition with column pivoting.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Pivoting
The largest-magnitude element of the first column is $3$ (row 2). Row swap: $PA = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, $P\vec b = (6,5)^T$. (This avoids large multipliers and rounding errors.)

Step 2: Decomposition PA = LU
Multiplier $l_{21} = \frac13$. $R_2 \to R_2 - \frac13R_1$: $(0,\ 2 - \tfrac43) = (0,\tfrac23)$. $L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \tfrac13 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $U = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 0 & \tfrac23 \end{pmatrix}$. Check: $LU = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 1 & \tfrac43 + \tfrac23 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ ✓.

Step 3: Forward and back substitution
$L\vec y = P\vec b$: $y_1 = 6$, $\frac13\cdot6 + y_2 = 5 \Rightarrow y_2 = 3$. $U\vec x = \vec y$: $\frac23x_2 = 3 \Rightarrow x_2 = \frac92$; $3x_1 + 4\cdot\frac92 = 6 \Rightarrow x_1 = -4$.

Step 4: Check
$\vec x = (-4;\ 4.5)^T$: $-4 + 2\cdot4.5 = 5$ ✓ and $3\cdot(-4) + 4\cdot4.5 = 6$ ✓. Advantage of the LU decomposition: for further right-hand sides two triangular solves suffice.

exercises.title: Euler and Runge-Kutta methods
exercises.description: Consider $y' = y$, $y(0) = 1$ (exact $y = e^x$). Compute $y(0.1)$ with one step $h = 0.1$ by (a) Euler, (b) Heun, (c) classical Runge-Kutta (order $4$) and compare with $e^{0.1} = 1.105171$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Euler
$y_1 = y_0 + hf(x_0,y_0) = 1 + 0.1\cdot1 = 1.1$. Error $5.2\cdot10^{-3}$.

Step 4: Comparison of orders
Error: Euler $5\cdot10^{-3}$ (order $1$), Heun $2\cdot10^{-4}$ (order $2$), RK4 $\approx 8\cdot10^{-8}$ (order $4$). Halving $h$ reduces the global error by a factor of $2$, $4$ and $16$ respectively.
